items.title: GDPR, the EU AI Act & ISO 27001: AI Compliance in Europe
items.summary: Europe sets standards that increasingly shape how organizations operate globally, not just inside the EU. Three frameworks cover most of it. Terms covered: - GDPR: governs how personal data of EU residents is collected, stored, processed and protected, and applies to any organization handling that data regardless of where it is based. Automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals requires transparency and human oversight. - EU AI Act: the first comprehensive regulatory framework for AI, taking a risk-based approach. Some uses are prohibited outright, low-risk applications face minimal requirements, and high-risk systems in hiring, credit scoring, healthcare and law enforcement face strict obligations. - ISO 27001: the internationally recognized standard for information security management, often a baseline expectation in European enterprise procurement Together these define what responsible AI deployment looks like in Europe. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #GDPR #EUAIAct #ISO27001 #AICompliance #AIGlossary #H2Oai

items.title: ToyBlocks: Our first Foundation World for robotics learning and evaluation
items.summary: To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

items.title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
items.summary: What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? Ioannis Zempekakis, Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark. Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like hydra heads. From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide. items.title: Integrating quantum and high-performance computing: Co-design platform for quantum error correction
items.summary: Caption:IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Quantum Science Center (QSC), and AMD have launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction that brings quantum and high-performance computing together in a single environment: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-11-05-oak-ridge-national-lab,-ibm,-and-amd-launch-new-co-design-platform-for-quantum-error-correction The platform pairs IBM’s 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor with ORNL’s Umbra supercomputing system, powered by AMD Instinct™ GPUs and AMD EPYC™ CPUs, to help researchers develop and test the quantum-classical workflows needed for large-scale quantum error correction. By co-locating quantum and classical computing resources, researchers can explore faster decoding, optimize error correction techniques, and advance the infrastructure required for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. The initiative supports the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission and its goal of enabling scientifically relevant quantum computing by 2028.

items.title: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, IBM, and AMD launch co-design platform for quantum error correction
items.summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it.In response to meet this challenge, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and @AMD have unveiled a new co-design platform for quantum error correction, with its initial deployment in IBM’s quantum facility in New York: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/ornl-amd-error-correction-co-design-platform Engineered to help researchers advance quantum error correction techniques within the workflows they will ultimately support, the co-design platform pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processors with ORNL’s Umbra high-performance computing (HPC) system, which is comprised of AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and AMD Turin CPUs. These systems form a co-located environment that is connected to ORNL’s broader supercomputing ecosystem.

items.title: Why AI Agents Need Their Own 70,000-Year-Old Language Revolution (with Vijoy Pandey)
items.summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041
